beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Kavya, and this video is about ontologies for observability at scale. This narration is AI-generated with Kokoro text-to-speech, reading a script I wrote and reviewed. At ten services, everyone just knows what 'payment service' means. At a thousand, three teams tag three different things 'payments,' and an agent asking what depends on it gets a confident wrong answer. Here's what actually fixes that.

props.command: At ten services, everyone just knows what 'payment-service' means. At a thousand, three teams tag three different things 'payments' and an agent asking what depends on it gets a wrong graph with total confidence. Is a bigger model going to fix that, or is this a modeling problem?
output: same word, three different services, zero agreement
one canonical entity, three teams' telemetry mapped into it
it's a modeling problem, not a model problem

beats.narration_text: Here's the idea: an ontology for observability isn't a naming convention. It's a shared model of what things are and how they relate. Naming is the easy part — the relationships are the whole point.

props.text:
An ontology for observability is a naming convention.
Actually — it's a shared model of what things ARE.
Naming is the easy part.
props.replacementWords: a shared model of what things ARE

beats.narration_text: Strip it down and it's four things. Entity types — what counts as a service, a deployment, a dependency. Relationships — calls, owns, depends-on, modeled instead of implied. Stable identifiers, so the same service is the same service everywhere. And a shared vocabulary every team's telemetry maps into. This is what scale actually breaks.

beats.narration_text: Watch what happens without one. Team A's traces call it payment-svc. Team B calls it PaymentService. Team C's "payments" resource is secretly three separate services. Ask an agent what depends on the payment service, and it can only see one of three — with full confidence.

shot.visual_intent: Output-only terminal card, no source shown. The three naming variants print, then the agent's incomplete answer lands last.

beats.narration_text: With one, all three map to a single canonical entity, stable ID and all. The same question now resolves against the real dependency graph — all three teams' services, correctly merged, not guessed at.

shot.visual_intent: Output-only terminal card, no source shown. The canonical entity and its mapped variants print, then the complete agent answer lands last.

beats.narration_text: Recap: an observability ontology is entity types, relationships, stable identifiers, and a shared vocabulary. Without it, three teams and three names leave an agent seeing a third of the real graph. With it, every team's telemetry maps into one canonical entity, and the graph is actually complete. The honest boundary: an ontology can't reason about a span that was never emitted. It fixes meaning, not missing instrumentation.

artifactLines: An observability ontology = entity types + relationships + stable identifiers + a shared vocabulary.
Without it: three teams, three names, one agent that only sees a third of the real graph.
With it: every team's telemetry maps into one canonical entity — the graph is actually complete.
Boundary: an ontology can't reason about a span that was never emitted. It fixes meaning, not missing instrumentation.
